To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the protein kinase C isozymes are activated by diacylglycerols that are produced by receptor stimulated hydrolysis of the membrane lipid phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphos­ phate.

the protein kinases that regulate synaptic transmission and synaptic plasticity are activated by Ca 2+ /calmo­ din, Ca 2+, and cAMP and that the Ca 2+ -activated and Ca 2+ and cAMP- activated kinases are regulated by phosphorylation.
the protein kinase that is activated by cGMP is a member of a large family of enzymes that phosphorylate proteins on serine and threonine residues.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular and cellular mechanisms by which nerve cells encode information and store it for periods of time ranging from a few minutes to many hours.
the molecular mechanisms of memory.
the molecular and cellular basis for learning and memory, and with the molecular mechanisms that underlie the development of the nervous system.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the molecular mechanisms of memory formation are not yet understood.

the CaM kinase and the cAMP-dependent kinase, the two protein kinases that have been studied most extensively in the nervous system and that are the subject of this review, are involved in the regulation of a variety of cellular pro­ cesses.

the molecular mechanisms for short-term memory are the second-messenger induced activation of protein kinases and the phosphoryla- tion-dependent modulation of the function of ion channels and other proteins in nerve cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have been able to identify and isolate a protein kinase from rat brain that can be phosphorylated by Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase and that can then be phosphorylated by cAMP-dependent protein kinase.
the protein kinase C isozymes, the protein kinase A and the protein kinase B are all important for memory.
the second messenger systems are involved in the regulation of neuronal plasticity, which is the cellular basis for learning and memory.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain has the ability to learn new information and to store it in a form that is not dependent on the continued presence of the information.
we can now use this information to design drugs that can target these enzymes and help us to treat diseases like Alzheimer’s disease.
the protein kinase A (PKA) signaling cascade is essential to memory formation.
